prompt: What makes a report a compliance report, in the lesson's sense?

choices.text: It is long and goes to the board
choices.why: The board is inside the company; it chooses its own reports.

choices.text: Outsiders set its terms
choices.why: Right: the company supplies evidence for a decision that belongs to someone else.

choices.text: It is produced by the legal department instead of by BI
choices.why: Legal and compliance interpret the rule; the numbers are produced by BI, the same way every time.

choices.text: It contains personal data
choices.why: Many internal reports do too; what defines compliance is who requires the report.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson give as an example of an outside body and what it receives?

choices.text: The ANPD receives every company's monthly sales
choices.why: The ANPD enforces the data protection law; sales go to the tax authority.

choices.text: The Central Bank receives Varanda's stock levels
choices.why: A retailer's stock is nobody's regulatory business at the Central Bank.

choices.text: The Central Bank receives data on a lender's loans through the SCR
choices.why: Right: and the Central Bank sets how those loans are classified.

choices.text: Hospitals send their bed occupancy to the tax authority every month so it can check their prices
choices.why: The lesson names notifications to health surveillance and reporting for SUS patients, not this.

prompt: The rule behind a regulatory report can be read two ways, and the two readings give different numbers. What does the lesson say the analyst should do?
hint: The definition is not yours to choose.

choices.text: Pick the reading that gives the better number and note it in the file
choices.why: A flattering choice made alone is exactly what a regulator questions later.

choices.text: Report both numbers and let the regulator choose
choices.why: A report has one answer per field; the ambiguity has to be settled before it is filled.

choices.text: Get a written answer from compliance or the regulator
choices.why: Right: the written answer becomes part of the definition the report is produced from.

choices.text: Use whichever reading last year's report used, without asking
choices.why: Consistency helps, but an unchecked habit is not a definition anybody approved.

prompt: Which of these change for an analyst when a report is regulatory rather than internal? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The definition is copied from the rule, with its version
choices.why: Right: it is not the company's to write.

choices.text: The work is planned backwards from the deadline
choices.why: Right: a day late carries a penalty.

choices.text: The report has to be drawn as a dashboard
choices.why: The form is the regulator's file format, not a dashboard.

choices.text: Each number must be producible again years later
choices.why: Right: the report is evidence.

prompt: In the twelve loans, what percentage of the balance is 30 or more days overdue, to one decimal?
Counted in loans rather than in reais, what percentage of the twelve loans is 90 or more days overdue, to one decimal?
At a meeting, the board sees "default 10.5%" and the collections team shows "default 32.7%" for the same loans. Which is right?

choices.text: 10.5%, because it is the regulator's and therefore the true one
choices.why: The regulator's definition is binding for the report, not truer for the collections team's job.

choices.text: Both, under different definitions that need different names
choices.why: Right: 90+ for the report, 30+ for collections; the problem is the shared label.

choices.text: 32.7%, because it warns earlier
choices.why: Warning earlier is its purpose, not proof that the other is wrong.

choices.text: Neither: the two should be averaged into one figure for the board
choices.why: An average matches no definition at all, which is one of the three wrong ways out.

prompt: A director has already shown the board an internal arrears figure, and asks Lívia's counterpart at Ipê to make the regulatory report "consistent" with it. What does the lesson say?
hint: Which number may never be edited?

choices.text: Adjust the regulatory figure slightly, since both describe the same loans
choices.why: Editing the outside number turns a labelling problem into a false report.

choices.text: Stop reporting the internal figure
choices.why: The collections team needs the early warning; dropping it is another wrong way out.

choices.text: Ask the regulator to accept the 30-day definition this time
choices.why: The rule is the same for every lender; the company cannot negotiate its definition per report.

choices.text: Refuse; rename the internal figure and show the two together, labelled
choices.why: Right: keep both, label both, never reconcile by editing.

prompt: Wherever an outside rule defines a number, the internal version gets a different ___, so the two are never read as one.
After loan 6's late payment is entered with its real date, it was 70 days overdue at 31 December. Re-run on live data, what share of the balance is 90+ days overdue, to one decimal?
hint: Only loan 9 is left in the 90+ column.

prompt: Ipê filed 10.5% and the same query now says 3.9%. What does the lesson say about the two numbers?

choices.text: The filed number was an error and must be corrected at once
choices.why: It was right on what Ipê knew when it filed; a correction follows the rule's own process, if any.

choices.text: The query has a bug, since a query must always give the same answer
choices.why: The query is fine; the live tables it reads changed.

choices.text: Both are correct; only a frozen snapshot reproduces the filed one
choices.why: Right: live data keeps changing after the date the report is about.

choices.text: The lower number should have been filed
choices.why: The payment had not been entered when Ipê filed; nobody could have known.

prompt: Put the path from the source systems to a submitted report in order.
hint: Everything after the snapshot is fixed.
items: The source systems record the loans
A nightly copy brings the data into the warehouse
A snapshot is frozen as at the reporting date
A versioned definition computes the report from the snapshot
A named person approves the exact file, which is submitted
trap: Computing the report from the nightly copy and freezing afterwards means the filed number came from data nobody kept.

prompt: A correction to December's data arrives in March, after the December report was filed. By the lesson, what happens to the December snapshot?

choices.text: It is updated, so that it is accurate
choices.why: Then the filed number could never be produced again.

choices.text: It stays as it was; the correction goes into a later period or a formal resubmission
choices.why: Right: the snapshot is what Ipê knew when it filed.

choices.text: It is deleted and replaced by a new snapshot
choices.why: Deleting it destroys the evidence for a report already sent.

choices.text: It is merged with March's snapshot
choices.why: Mixing dates produces a snapshot of no date at all.

prompt: Lívia follows customers' orders using a code in place of the name; the key to the codes is in another table. Under the LGPD, what is her data?

choices.text: Pseudonymised, and still personal data
choices.why: Right: the company can turn the code back into a person.

choices.text: Anonymised, so the LGPD no longer applies
choices.why: Anonymised means it cannot be linked back by reasonable means; here the key exists.

choices.text: Sensitive personal data, because purchase histories are sensitive
choices.why: Purchases are ordinary personal data; the sensitive category covers things like health.

choices.text: Public data, because customers gave it to Varanda willingly when they placed their orders online
choices.why: Giving data to a company for a purpose does not make it public.

prompt: A table of individual purchases has the customer code removed but keeps the date, the store and the exact basket. Is it anonymised, by the lesson's test?
hint: What could somebody with the file work out?

choices.text: Yes, because no identifier at all is left in it once the code is gone
choices.why: Removing identifiers is not enough when the remaining fields point at one person.

choices.text: Yes, as soon as the file leaves Varanda's own systems
choices.why: Where the file sits changes nothing about what it reveals.

choices.text: Not necessarily: date, store and basket may point at a person
choices.why: Right: art. 12's exception is anonymisation that can be reversed.

choices.text: No, because only health data can ever be anonymised
choices.why: Any personal data can be anonymised if it truly cannot be linked back.

prompt: A borrower asks Ipê to delete their data. Their loans are in the frozen snapshots a regulator may ask to see. What does the lesson describe?
hint: The law allows keeping data for a legal obligation.

choices.text: Delete the borrower from every snapshot and every copy Ipê holds
choices.why: That edits the evidence behind reports already filed, which an obligation requires keeping.

choices.text: Refuse the request, since Ipê is a regulated company and its data is exempt
choices.why: Being regulated covers what an obligation requires, not every copy Ipê holds.

choices.text: Keep the required snapshot apart; delete the convenience copies
choices.why: Right: and which record falls under which obligation is decided once, in writing, by compliance and legal.

choices.text: Replace the name with a code
choices.why: Pseudonymising keeps the data personal and does not answer a deletion request.

prompt: Match each habit to the question that sounds like it.
hint: The middle column of the table.

pairs.right: What will you decide with this?
Per what, and did it move?
Today, this month or this year?

pairs.left: A number that can be produced again
pairs.right: Which snapshot, which version, who approved?

prompt: Which course of the `bi` track takes the spreadsheet further, with lookups and pivot tables?
hint: The next course in the track.

choices.text: statistics
choices.why: That one is the mathematics: variation, sampling, regression.

choices.text: data-governance
choices.why: That one is law, quality, lineage and audit.

choices.text: excel-analytics
choices.why: Right: lookups, SUMIFS, pivot tables and dashboards in Excel.

choices.text: data-storytelling
choices.why: That one is showing the answer to the right person.

prompt: Before any tool, the course's first habit is to ask what somebody will ___ with the answer.
Which of these are among the four things the lesson says make a number reproducible? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A snapshot that is never updated
choices.why: Right: the report reads it, never the live tables.

choices.text: The definition's version recorded with each submission
choices.why: Right: last year's submissions were made with last year's version.

choices.text: A dashboard that refreshes every hour
choices.why: Fresh data is the opposite of what a filed number needs.

choices.text: A record of who approved which file, and when
choices.why: Right: the start of an audit trail.

choices.text: Rounding every figure to whole numbers
choices.why: Rounding does not make a number reproducible; a fixed input and a fixed method do.

prompt: Asked of compliance reporting, what is the typical trap in lesson 17's four questions?

choices.text: Missing the deadline
choices.why: A real risk, handled by planning backwards; the trap the lesson names is about definitions.

choices.text: Using a spreadsheet for a regulatory file instead of a BI tool built for the purpose
choices.why: The tool is not the trap; the snapshot, version and approval matter in any tool.

choices.text: Two numbers with one name, quietly made to agree
choices.why: Right: the outside one and the inside one, reconciled by editing.

choices.text: Reporting too many indicators to the regulator
choices.why: The regulator decides what is reported; the company does not choose how many.

prompt: Varanda's year-end sales figure is internal, not regulatory. Why does the lesson still suggest a frozen snapshot of 31 December?

choices.text: It is the kind of number somebody asks to see again
choices.why: Right: the habit is worth taking back into internal work wherever a number will be quoted later.

choices.text: Because the tax authority requires the sales snapshot
choices.why: The tax filing has its own records; the lesson's reason is about the board's figure.

choices.text: To stop late sales being recorded
choices.why: The live tables keep recording; the snapshot just keeps what was known.

choices.text: Because Helena dislikes numbers that change after she has presented them to the board
choices.why: The reason is reproducibility, not taste.
